# File-type filtering in ripgrep

ripgrep's `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear` and
`--type-list` flags are all backed by a single small subsystem in the
`ignore` crate: `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`. This document walks through how
a type definition is represented, how `TypesBuilder` turns a set of
definitions and selections into a matcher, and where the CLI plugs into it.

## Representing a type definition

A file type is nothing more than a name plus a list of globs:

```rust
pub struct FileTypeDef {
    name: String,
    globs: Vec<String>,
}
```

The full set of built-in types lives in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`
as a hand-maintained, lexicographically sorted, `#[rustfmt::skip]` constant:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["ada"], &["*.adb", "*.ads"]),
    ...
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    ...
];
```

Each entry pairs one or more *names* (aliases such as `bat`/`batch`) with the
globs that define the type. `TypesBuilder::add_defaults` walks this table and
calls `add(name, glob)` once per name/glob pair, so aliases end up as fully
independent `FileTypeDef` entries in the builder's map rather than references
to a shared definition.

`TypesBuilder` itself holds the definitions in a `HashMap<String,
FileTypeDef>`, keyed by name, plus a separate `Vec<Selection<()>>` recording
what the user asked for:

```rust
pub struct TypesBuilder {
    types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>,
    selections: Vec<Selection<()>>,
}

enum Selection<T> {
    Select(String, T),
    Negate(String, T),
}
```

`add(name, glob)` appends a glob to (or creates) the named definition, and
rejects a `name` that isn't purely alphanumeric or that equals `"all"`
(`"all"` is reserved as the wildcard selector). `add_def` is the string form
used by `--type-add`, supporting two grammars: `name:glob` and
`name:include:other,names` — the latter copies every glob from each named
type into the new one at add time (not lazily), and fails fast if any
referenced type doesn't already exist. `select`/`negate` push a
`Selection::Select`/`Selection::Negate` onto `selections`; both special-case
the name `"all"` by expanding it to one selection per currently-defined type.

Note what `TypesBuilder` does *not* do: it never validates that a selected
name actually exists in `types` until `build()` runs. `select("rust")`
succeeds unconditionally even if `rust` was never defined.

## Building a matcher

`TypesBuilder::build()` compiles the map of definitions plus the list of
selections into an immutable `Types`:

```rust
pub struct Types {
    defs: Vec<FileTypeDef>,
    selections: Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>,
    has_selected: bool,
    glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>,
    set: GlobSet,
    matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>,
}
```

The build walks `self.selections` in the order they were pushed (i.e., the
order flags appeared on the command line). For each one it looks up the
`FileTypeDef` by name — an unknown name is where `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`
is actually raised — then adds every glob in that definition to a single
shared `GlobSetBuilder`, using `.literal_separator(true)` (so `*` won't cross
a `/`). `glob_to_selection` is a parallel vector recording, for every glob
inserted into the set, which selection and which glob-within-that-definition
it came from. `has_selected` is true iff at least one selection is a
`Select` (as opposed to only `Negate`s) — this drives whitelist-vs-blacklist
behavior at match time.

Everything is compiled into one `GlobSet` regardless of how many types are
selected; there's no per-type matcher. Precedence between overlapping globs
falls entirely out of insertion order: `GlobSet::matches_into` returns the
indices of every glob that matched, and `Types::matched` takes `matches.last()`
as authoritative — "the highest precedent match is the last one" (the
in-source comment). Since selections were inserted in command-line order,
*later flags win* when two selected/negated types both match the same file.

`matches: Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>` is a `regex-automata` object pool that hands
out reusable `Vec<usize>` scratch buffers for `matches_into`, avoiding an
allocation per `matched()` call under concurrent walking (`Types` is cloned
into every worker thread via `Arc`, see `ignore::WalkBuilder`/`WalkParallel`).

## Matching a path

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob<'_>>`, ripgrep's
three-valued `None`/`Ignore(_)`/`Whitelist(_)` result used throughout the
`ignore` crate. The logic:

1. Directories and an empty glob set never match (`Match::None`) — type
   filtering only ever applies to files.
2. Only the *file name* (`pathutil::file_name`) is matched, not the full
   path — a type glob like `*.rs` never sees the directory component. A path
   with no file name component is `Ignore` if any type is selected, else
   `None`.
3. If any glob in the set matches, the *last* matching index wins; its
   selection determines `Ignore` (negated) or `Whitelist` (selected).
4. If nothing matched but `has_selected` is true, the result is
   `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` — this is the whitelist behavior: once
   you've selected at least one type, anything that doesn't match any
   selected type is implicitly excluded, even if it isn't explicitly
   negated.
5. If nothing matched and nothing was selected (only negations, or no
   selections at all), the result is `Match::None` — negation alone doesn't
   turn on whitelist mode.

`Types` is consulted from `ignore::dir::Ignore::matched` (`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`),
*after* override globs (`-g/--glob`) and ignore-file rules have both had a
chance to produce a definitive `Ignore`/`Whitelist`, but not overriding a
whitelist those layers produced — types are lowest precedence among the
three. `-g/--glob` still wins over `-t/--type` even when the flags target the
same file, which is documented directly on the `Type` flag.

## Where the CLI plugs in

The flag layer never touches `TypesBuilder` directly. `-t`, `-T`,
`--type-add` and `--type-clear` each just push a `TypeChange` variant
(`Select`, `Negate`, `Add`, `Clear`) onto `LowArgs::type_changes`
(`crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs`), preserving command-line order. `--type-list`
instead sets `args.mode = Mode::Types`, short-circuiting search entirely.

`crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types()` is the one place all of this is
assembled: it creates a `TypesBuilder`, calls `add_defaults()`, then replays
`type_changes` in order — `Clear`/`Add`/`Select`/`Negate` map straight onto
the builder's like-named methods — and calls `build()`. The resulting `Types`
is cached on `HiArgs` and handed to `WalkBuilder::types` (`crates/ignore/src/walk.rs`),
which stores it on the shared `ignore::dir::IgnoreBuilder` state that every
directory-walk thread clones from.

## What a contributor needs to know

- **Adding a built-in type** means editing `default_types.rs` directly and
  keeping the list lexicographically sorted and 79-columns-wrapped per its
  header comment — there's no code generator.
- **Order is meaningful and is preserved end-to-end**: CLI argument order →
  `type_changes` → `selections` → `glob_to_selection` → last-match-wins. A
  test worth reading before changing this path is
  `defs.rs::test_type_not`, which asserts `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` preserves
  interleaved order in `type_changes`.
- **`clear` only removes a definition, not a selection.** `TypesBuilder::clear`
  removes an entry from `self.types`; if a prior `select`/`negate` already
  named it, `build()` will fail with `Error::UnrecognizedFileType` when it
  looks the name up. `--type-clear` is meant to precede `--type-add` for the
  same name, not to retroactively cancel a `-t`.
- **`include` definitions copy, they don't reference.** `add_def("src:include:cpp,py,md")`
  clones the current globs of `cpp`, `py`, and `md` into `src` at that point
  in argument processing. A later `--type-add` to `cpp` will not retroactively
  extend `src`.
- **Type names are validated, glob syntax is not, until `build()`.** `add`
  rejects non-alphanumeric names immediately, but a malformed glob only
  surfaces as `Error::Glob` inside `build()`, since compiling globs is
  deferred to `GlobSetBuilder::build()`.
- **Matching is filename-only.** Anyone tempted to write a type whose glob
  assumes a path segment (e.g. `src/*.rs`) needs to know `literal_separator(true)`
  is set and only the final component is even passed to the matcher.
- Behavioral changes here are exercised by the table-driven tests at the
  bottom of `types.rs` (the `matched!` macro) and by the flag-level tests
  colocated with each flag in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs` — both are cheap
  places to add a regression case before touching `Types::matched` or
  `TypesBuilder::build`.

# File-type filtering in `ignore::types`

ripgrep's `-t/--type` filtering lives in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with
the built-in type list in `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. This module
is independent of gitignore matching (`gitignore.rs`) and glob overrides
(`overrides.rs`); the three are combined only in `crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`,
where a directory walk decides whether to descend into or skip a path.

## Representing a type definition

A file type is a `FileTypeDef`: a `name: String` plus a `globs: Vec<String>`
(`types.rs:146`). There's no glob compilation at this stage — `FileTypeDef`
just stores raw glob strings, with `Clone + Eq + PartialEq` derived so
definitions can be compared and copied cheaply. Its `name()`/`globs()`
accessors are how `--type-list` prints each type (`crates/core/main.rs:332`
iterates `args.types().definitions()`).

Definitions accumulate in a `TypesBuilder`, which holds a
`HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` keyed by name plus a separate
`Vec<Selection<()>>` recording which types the caller wants to filter on
(`types.rs:305`). Three ways to populate the map:

- `add(name, glob)` pushes one glob onto `name`'s `FileTypeDef`, creating it
  if absent. `name` must not be `"all"` and every character must be
  `is_alphanumeric()`, or it returns `Error::InvalidDefinition`
  (`types.rs:417`) — this is why `--type-add 'foo-bar:*.x'` is rejected.
- `add_def(spec)` parses ripgrep's colon-delimited definition string, used
  by `--type-add`. Splitting on `:` accepts two shapes (`types.rs:442`):
  `name:glob`, or `name:include:other,names`, which copies every glob from
  each named existing type into `name`. All referenced names are checked to
  exist *before* anything is added, so a bad include fails atomically rather
  than partially populating `name`.
- `add_defaults()` walks the `DEFAULT_TYPES` table and calls `add` for every
  `(names, globs)` pair, so one glob list can register under several
  aliases (`bat`/`batch` both map to `*.bat`, `cs`/`csharp` to `*.cs`).

`clear(name)` removes a definition outright (`--type-clear`) via a plain
`HashMap::remove`. `select(name)`/`negate(name)` don't touch `types` at all
— they append `Selection::Select`/`Negate(name, ())` to `self.selections`
(`types.rs:381`, `:395`). The `()` payload is resolved at build time.
`name == "all"` expands to one selection per key currently in the map, so
`--type=all`'s effect depends on what's been defined *before* it on the
command line.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build()` (`types.rs:322`) turns selections and definitions
into a matcher. For each `Selection`, in order, it looks up the named
`FileTypeDef`, compiles every glob with
`GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true).build()`, and adds it to a
shared `GlobSetBuilder`. A side table, `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize,
usize)>`, maps each compiled glob's index back to `(selection index, glob
index within that def)`; `has_selected` records whether any selection is a
`Select` rather than only `Negate`s. An unresolvable selection name returns
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType` — the runtime counterpart to `add_def`'s
ahead-of-time check for `include:`.

The resulting `Types` holds the sorted `defs`, resolved `selections` (now
carrying `FileTypeDef` instead of `()`), `has_selected`, `glob_to_selection`,
the compiled `GlobSet`, and a `Pool<Vec<usize>>` scratch buffer so
`matched()` doesn't allocate per call. `literal_separator(true)` is a real
behavioral choice: `*` won't cross a `/`, though it rarely matters since
matching happens against the file name alone (see below).

## Matching

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` (`types.rs:261`) never matches directories,
and an empty glob set short-circuits to `Match::None`. Otherwise it extracts
just the file name via `pathutil::file_name` — type globs never see
directory components — and queries the `GlobSet`. Multiple globs can match;
`Types` takes `matches.last()`, the highest-index one, as highest
precedence. Since globs are added in `self.selections` order, a later
`--type`/`--type-not` on the command line wins over an earlier one for the
same file.

Once the winning glob's selection is known, `sel.is_negated()` decides the
outcome: a negated match is `Match::Ignore`, otherwise `Match::Whitelist`.
If nothing matched, the fallback is `Match::Ignore` when `has_selected` is
true (some `--type` was given, so anything else is out) or `Match::None`
when only `--type-not` selections exist (stay neutral, let other matchers
decide).

## Where it fits in a directory walk

`Types` alone doesn't decide whether ripgrep searches a file. `dir.rs`'s
`Ignore::matched` composes it with overrides and ignore rules in fixed
precedence: overrides (`-g/--glob`) first and decisive either way, then
gitignore-style rules (short-circuiting only on `Ignore`, since a gitignore
*whitelist* still needs to survive type filtering), then `Types::matched`
last (`dir.rs:376`–`408`), with any ignore-rule whitelist held in a local
and returned only if types don't override it. The `-t/--type` flag's own doc
states this precedence explicitly: it "has lower precedence than both the
`--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files"
(`crates/core/flags/defs.rs:6795`).

## What a contributor needs to know

- **CLI flags are thin.** `-t`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear`
  each just push a `TypeChange` variant onto `LowArgs::type_changes`
  (`crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs:749`), preserving command-line order. The
  builder is assembled once in `hiargs.rs`'s `types()`: `add_defaults()`
  first, then every `TypeChange` replayed in order — interleaving matters,
  since `--type-clear rust --type-add 'rust:*.rs'` differs from the flags
  reversed.
- **Two distinct error paths.** `Error::InvalidDefinition` is a malformed
  `add_def` string or non-alphanumeric name, caught at `add`/`add_def` time;
  `Error::UnrecognizedFileType` is a `select`/`negate`/`include:` naming an
  undefined type, caught at `build()` or `add_def()`. Keep that split if you
  touch validation — it's user-visible in error messages.
- **Adding a default type** means editing `DEFAULT_TYPES`, kept
  lexicographically sorted and wrapped to 79 columns per its doc comment.
  Duplicate globs across aliases are intentional.
- **Matching is name-only**; a change that lets `matched()` see directory
  components would be a real behavior break.
- **Precedence is encoded twice** — operationally in `dir.rs` and in prose
  in `Type`'s `doc_long`. Changing the composition order means updating both.
- **`Types` clones cheaply on purpose**: the `Arc<Pool<...>>` scratch buffer
  and pre-built `GlobSet` let it be shared across parallel walk threads
  without rebuilding.

# File-type filtering in `ignore`

File-type filtering (`rg -t rust`, `-T cpp`, `--type-add`) lives entirely in
`crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, backed by a static table of built-ins in
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`. It's one of three independent matchers
`ignore::dir::Ignore` consults per path — the others being glob overrides
(`-g`) and gitignore-style files — and it has the lowest precedence of the
three.

## Representing a type definition

A type is a name plus a list of globs (`FileTypeDef { name: String, globs:
Vec<String> }`). `default_types.rs` supplies these as a flat,
lexicographically sorted static table, `DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])]`,
pairing one or more names with one or more globs — the array-of-names form
is how one glob set gets registered under aliases, e.g.
`(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`.

`TypesBuilder` accumulates definitions before anything is compiled:

- `add(name, glob)` inserts one glob under `name`, rejecting `name == "all"`
  or any non-alphanumeric character. `all` is reserved as the "select
  everything" pseudo-type, and CLI-facing names must round-trip through
  `--type`/`--type-not` without a delimiter clash.
- `add_def(spec)` parses the CLI string form. `"name:glob"` is a plain
  addition; `"name:include:other1,other2"` copies every glob already
  registered under `other1` and `other2` into `name`, evaluated once at
  `add_def` time — a later `add` or `clear` on `other1` does not
  retroactively change `name`. Malformed input (wrong colon count, an
  unknown included name, empty parts) is validated before any definition is
  mutated.
- `clear(name)` removes a definition from the builder's `types` map. It does
  **not** remove any `select`/`negate` selection already queued that
  references that name; a stale selection is only caught later, at
  `build()`, as `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`.
- `add_defaults()` loads the whole `DEFAULT_TYPES` table.

None of this touches matching yet: `TypesBuilder` is pure bookkeeping over a
`HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>`.

## Selections and building the matcher

Filtering is driven by a second list, `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`, built
by `select(name)` / `negate(name)`, where `Selection<T>` is `Select(String,
T)` or `Negate(String, T)`. `"all"` is special-cased in both methods to
expand to a selection of every name currently in `self.types` — so
`--type=all` only picks up types defined before it *within the builder's
in-memory map*, which in practice means every `--type-add` already parsed,
since `TypesBuilder::build()` runs once after all flags are read.

`build()` turns the loose definitions and selections into a `Types`:

1. `has_selected = selections.iter().any(|s| !s.is_negated())` — true if at
   least one plain (non-negated) selection exists. This flips the meaning of
   "no glob matched" from *no opinion* to *ignored* (see below).
2. For each selection, in order, its `FileTypeDef` is looked up by name
   (error if absent), and each of its globs is added to a single
   `GlobSetBuilder`, with `literal_separator(true)` so `*` never crosses a
   `/`.
3. `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>` maps a glob's index in the
   compiled `GlobSet` back to `(selection index, glob index)` — the only way
   to recover which selection produced a match, since `GlobSet` itself only
   returns match indices.

The resulting `Types` holds the compiled `GlobSet`, that index map, the
resolved selections, `has_selected`, and a `Pool<Vec<usize>>` used to reuse
the scratch buffer `GlobSet::matches_into` writes into, so `matched()`
doesn't allocate per call.

## Matching a path

`Types::matched(path, is_dir) -> Match<Glob>` is the entry point, where
`Match<T>` (`crates/ignore/src/lib.rs`) is the three-way result shared by
every matcher in the crate: `None`, `Ignore(T)`, `Whitelist(T)`.

- Directories, and an empty glob set, short-circuit to `Match::None` — type
  filtering applies only to file names, never directly to traversal
  decisions (traversal is pruned indirectly, once a descendant file would be
  filtered).
- The path is reduced to its file name; a path with no file name component
  matches nothing, or is ignored outright if `has_selected` is true.
- `GlobSet::matches_into` collects every matching glob index for the name;
  `Types` looks only at the *last* one. `GlobSetBuilder` preserves insertion
  order, and insertion order here is selection order, so **the last
  `-t`/`-T` on the command line wins** when two selections' globs both match
  the same name.
- A match resolves to `Whitelist` or `Ignore` via `Selection::is_negated()`
  on its owning selection.
- No match resolves to `Ignore` if `has_selected` (something was positively
  selected and this file isn't one of those types), otherwise `None`.

This is why `-t rust -T cpp` reads as "rust only, and definitely not cpp"
rather than "rust minus cpp overlap": `has_selected` is set by the `-t`, so
every non-rust file is already ignored regardless of the `-T`.

## Precedence among matchers

`ignore::dir::Ignore::matched_ignore_or_dir` (`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`,
~line 380) checks overrides (`-g`/`--iglob`) first — an override match
returns immediately either way — then gitignore and custom-ignore-file
rules, and only if neither already decided to ignore the path does it
consult `self.0.types`. A whitelist from an earlier stage is remembered and
only overridden by a later stage's `Ignore`. This matches the `-t/--type`
flag's own doc comment in `crates/core/flags/defs.rs`: it "has lower
precedence than both the `--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore
files."

## Wiring from the CLI

`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` defines `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`,
`--type-add`, `--type-clear` and `--type-list` as thin handlers that each
push a `TypeChange` (`Clear`, `Add`, `Select`, `Negate`, in
`crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs`) onto `LowArgs::type_changes`, preserving
command-line order. `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types()` replays that list
against one `TypesBuilder` seeded with `add_defaults()`, then calls
`build()`. Because everything replays in a single pass after parsing,
order-dependent cases — `--type-clear` before or after a `--type-add` for
the same name, or `-t` before the `--type-add` defining it — resolve the way
a linear reading of the command line suggests.

## What a contributor needs to know

- New built-in types go in `default_types.rs`, kept sorted and wrapped at 79
  columns per its own header comment. `types.rs`'s `tests` module has a
  `matched!` macro for exercising selection/negation combinations — extend
  that table rather than writing ad hoc tests for a new type or `include:`
  chain.
- `clear()` not cascading into `selections` is a real footgun surface: don't
  assume clearing a definition invalidates a pending selection elsewhere —
  `build()`'s `Error::UnrecognizedFileType` is what currently catches that.
- "Last matching glob wins" falls directly out of `GlobSet` preserving
  insertion order and `Types` reading only `matches.last()`. Reordering
  selections before building the `GlobSetBuilder` would silently change
  which type wins on overlapping globs.

   meaning of "no glob matched" from *unopinionated* to *ignored* (see
   below).
2. For each selection, in order, look up its `FileTypeDef` by name (error if
   absent), and add each of its globs to a single `GlobSetBuilder`, with
   `literal_separator(true)` (so `*` in a glob never crosses a `/`).
3. `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>` maps a glob's index in the
   compiled `GlobSet` back to `(selection index, glob index within that
   definition)` — the only way to recover *which* selection a match came
   from, since `GlobSet` itself only returns indices.

The result, `Types`, holds the compiled `GlobSet`, the index map, the
resolved `Vec<Selection<FileTypeDef>>`, `has_selected`, and a `Pool<Vec<usize>>`
(from `regex_automata::util::pool`) used to reuse the `Vec` that
`GlobSet::matches_into` writes match indices into, so `matched()` doesn't
allocate per call.

## Matching a path

`Types::matched(path, is_dir) -> Match<Glob>` is the entry point. `Match<T>`
(`crates/ignore/src/lib.rs`) is the three-way result shared by every matcher
in the crate: `None` (no opinion), `Ignore(T)`, `Whitelist(T)`.

- Directories and an empty glob set both short-circuit to `Match::None` —
  type filtering only ever applies to file names, never to directory
  traversal decisions directly (traversal is pruned indirectly, once a
  descendant file would be filtered).
- The path is reduced to its file name (`pathutil::file_name`); a path
  without a file name component matches nothing, or is ignored outright if
  `has_selected` is true.
- `GlobSet::matches_into` collects **all** matching glob indices for the
  name. `Types` only looks at the *last* one — glob sets built by
  `GlobSetBuilder` preserve insertion order, and insertion order here is
  selection order, so **the last `-t`/`-T` flag on the command line wins**
  when two selections' globs both match the same file.
- If a glob matched: look up its owning selection via `glob_to_selection`,
  and return `Whitelist` or `Ignore` depending on `Selection::is_negated()`.
- If nothing matched: `Ignore` if `has_selected` (some type was positively
  selected and this file isn't one of them), otherwise `None` (no selections
  at all, or only negations — a file not matching any negated type is
  neither included nor excluded by type).

This is why `-t rust -T cpp` behaves as "rust only, and definitely not
cpp" rather than "rust minus cpp overlap": `has_selected` is set by the
`-t`, so every non-rust file — cpp or otherwise — is ignored; the `-T`
is redundant unless a `rust` definition and a `cpp` definition share globs
via `include:`.

## Precedence: where `Types` sits among the other matchers

`ignore::dir::Ignore::matched_ignore_or_dir` (`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs`,
~line 380) checks, in order: overrides (`-g`/`-i-glob`) first — an override
match returns immediately regardless of whitelist/ignore — then gitignore
and custom-ignore-file rules, then, only if neither of those already decided
to ignore the path, `self.0.types.matched(...)`. A whitelist result from an
earlier stage is remembered (`whitelisted`) and only overridden by a later
stage's `Ignore`. This mirrors the doc comment on the `-t/--type` flag in
`crates/core/flags/defs.rs`: "this flag has lower precedence than both the
`--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files."

## Wiring from the CLI

`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` defines `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`,
`--type-add`, `--type-clear`, and `--type-list` as thin flag handlers that
each push a `TypeChange` (`crates/core/flags/lowargs.rs`: `Clear`, `Add`,
`Select`, `Negate`) onto `LowArgs::type_changes`, preserving command-line
order. `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types()` replays that list against a
single `TypesBuilder` seeded with `add_defaults()`, then calls `build()`.
Because everything is replayed in one pass after argument parsing finishes,
order-dependent interactions — `--type-clear` before or after a
`--type-add` for the same name, or `-t` before the `--type-add` that defines
it — resolve the same way a linear reading of the command line suggests.

## What a contributor needs to know

- New built-in types go in `default_types.rs`, kept sorted and wrapped at 79
  columns per its own header comment; there's a doctest-adjacent unit test
  style in `types.rs`'s `tests` module (the `matched!` macro) for exercising
  selection/negation combinations — extend that table rather than writing
  ad hoc tests when adding coverage for a new type or an `include:` chain.
- `clear()` not cascading into `selections` is a real footgun surface: a
  future change to `TypesBuilder` should not assume clearing a definition
  also invalidates a pending selection, since `build()` is what currently
  catches that case via `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`.
- The "last matching glob wins" tie-break falls directly out of `GlobSet`
  preserving insertion order and `Types` only reading `matches.last()`;
  changing selection order (e.g. sorting selections before building the
  `GlobSetBuilder`) would silently change which type wins on overlapping
  globs.
"}

# Filtering searches by file type in ripgrep

When you search all day, you rarely want every file. You want the Rust, or the
Python, or everything except the minified JavaScript. ripgrep gives each file
format a short name and lets you filter on that name instead of retyping globs.
This guide covers the four flags that make it work: `--type`, `--type-not`,
`--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` (`-t`): keep only one kind of file

A file type is a name assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant
files. Instead of spelling out the extensions:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
```

you name the type:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The short form `-t` takes the type name with no space, so `-trust` reads as
"type rust." One name can stand in for a whole family of extensions. C source
and header files, for instance, both live under the `c` type, so `-tc` replaces
`-g '*.{c,h}'`.

You can pass `--type` more than once, and the results are combined: `rg -trust
-tpython` searches both. One caveat on precedence: `--type` ranks *below* both
the `--glob` flag and any rules found in ignore files. A `.gitignore` entry or
an explicit `--glob` can still exclude a file your type would otherwise match.

## `--type-not` (`-T`): exclude a kind of file

The mirror image excludes a type. To search everything but Rust:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type." The two compose: `rg -Trust -ttoml -Tjson` includes TOML while
excluding Rust and JSON.

### The special `all` type

Both flags accept the value `all`. `--type all` behaves as if you had passed
`--type` for every type ripgrep knows about, including any you added on the
command line. This is "whitelist" mode: ripgrep only searches files it
recognizes through a type definition. Conversely, `--type-not all` is
"blacklist" mode: only files that match *no* known type are searched.

The difference is sharper than it looks. Suppose your directory holds
`my-shell-script` (no extension) and `my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type
sh` and `rg --type all` search only `my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh`
type's globs match extensions, not bare names. But `rg --type-not all` searches
`my-shell-script` and skips `my-shell-library.bash`, since only the unextended
file is unrecognized.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types covering well-known open
formats. To see them all, with the globs behind each one:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line as a name, a colon, then a comma-delimited list
of its globs. Pipe it back through ripgrep to inspect one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

`--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags on the same
command line, so it is also how you confirm a custom type came out the way you
meant.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

When you keep reaching for the same group of formats, name it. Say you search
"web" files, meaning HTML, CSS, and JavaScript:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Each `--type-add` adds exactly one glob, so repeat the flag to build the type
up; or fold them into a single brace glob:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Defining a type and using it are separate steps. `--type-add 'web:...'` only
creates the name; `-tweb` then filters with it. The added globs join ripgrep's
built-in types rather than replacing them. Type names must be made of Unicode
letters or numbers only, with no punctuation.

You can also compose types from existing ones with the `include` directive,
listing other type names separated by commas:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc PATTERN
```

That makes `src` match C++, Python, and Markdown files at once. You can still
add more globs to it afterward with another `--type-add 'src:*.foo'`.

To start a type from scratch, `--type-clear NAME` drops every glob previously
defined for it; you can then add fresh globs after the clear.

### Nothing is saved

`--type-add` and `--type-clear` apply only to the command that carries them.
Type settings are not persisted. To make a custom type available everywhere,
put it in a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file so
every invocation picks it up.

# Filtering by file type

You search text for a living, so you already write the same globs over and over.
When you only want Rust files, you reach for `-g '*.rs'`. When you want C, you
reach for `-g '*.{c,h}'`, because you have to remember headers too. A file type
is just a name for one or more of those globs, so you write the name instead of
the pattern. ripgrep ships with a set of predefined types for well-known
formats, and you can add your own.

## `-t/--type`: search only one type

Point ripgrep at a type and it searches only files that match that type's
globs:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The short form takes its value with no space. A type is a name assigned to one
or more globs, so a single name can stand in for a broad set of extensions. The
`c` type covers both source and headers:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

Pass `-t` more than once and the types add up. `rg -trust -tmarkdown` searches
files matching either type.

Note that `--type` has lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and than any
rules found in ignore files. A type selection restricts what you search; it does
not override a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit glob.

There is one special value. `--type all` behaves as if you had passed `--type`
for every type ripgrep knows, including any you added on the command line. The
effect is a whitelist: ripgrep searches only files it recognizes and skips
everything else.

## `-T/--type-not`: exclude a type

Just as you can write a blacklist glob, you can blacklist a type:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type." Both flags stack, and you can mix them in one command
(`rg -Trust -ttoml -Tjson`).

`--type-not all` is the mirror of `--type all`: it excludes every recognized
type, leaving only files ripgrep does not recognize. That distinction turns on
file names, so it's worth a concrete case. Suppose you have `my-shell-script`
(no extension) and `my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type sh` and
`rg --type all` search only `my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh` type's
globs don't match a name without an extension. `rg --type-not all` does the
reverse: it searches `my-shell-script` and skips the `.bash` file.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

To see the types you can use, and the globs behind each one, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line, then a `:`, then a comma-delimited list of its
globs. Pipe the output back through ripgrep to find one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

The list reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags on the same command,
so it's also how you check that a type you defined came out the way you meant.

## `--type-add`: define your own

When a set of globs is yours and not one of the built-ins, name it. Say you
often search "web" files, meaning JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Each `--type-add` adds one glob, so you can pass the flag several times. A brace
pattern collapses that to one:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That defines the type `web`, applies it with `-tweb`, and searches for `title`.
The spec is `name:glob`, and type names may contain only Unicode letters or
numbers, no punctuation.

You can also build a type out of other types with the `include` directive. It
takes one or more existing type names, separated by commas, and pulls their
globs in:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
```

Add more globs to `src` afterward with another `--type-add 'src:*.foo'`. To
start a type over rather than extend it, clear it first with `--type-clear
<name>`, then add.

Note that `--type-add` applies only to the command you run it on. It does not
save anything; the next `rg` invocation won't know about `web`. To make a type
permanent, put it where every invocation sees it. A shell alias works:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

Or add the line to your ripgrep configuration file, which is the tidier home for
settings you always want:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

Either way, `--type-list` will then show `web` alongside the built-in types
every time.

# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

When you search the same kinds of files all day, typing out globs like
`-g '*.rs'` or `-g '*.{c,h}'` gets old fast. ripgrep's file-type filters give
those glob sets a name, so you can write `-trust` instead. This guide covers the
four flags you'll use: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` / `-t`: search only one kind of file

A *type* is just a name attached to one or more globs. `--type rust` (or the
short forms `-t rust` and `-trust`) tells ripgrep to search only files that
match the `rust` type's globs:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

Because a type can bundle several globs, one name often replaces an awkward
pattern. The `cpp` type, for instance, already covers headers and sources, so
`rg 'int main' -tcpp` beats spelling out `-g '*.{c,h}'`.

You can pass `--type` more than once to search several types at once:

```
$ rg TODO -trust -tpython
```

Two things worth knowing about precedence. First, `--type` is a *whitelist*:
once you name a type, ripgrep searches only matching files. Second, the flag has
lower precedence than both the `--glob` flag and any rules in your ignore files,
so a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit `-g` pattern still wins over a type
selection.

## `--type-not` / `-T`: skip a kind of file

The mirror image excludes a type instead of selecting it. `--type-not` (short
forms `-T` and `-Trust`) searches everything *except* the named type:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of this
type." You can mix them freely in one command; each flag is applied in order.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

ripgrep ships with more than two hundred predefined types, generally
corresponding to well-known formats. To see them all, along with the globs that
make up each one, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line as `name: glob, glob, ...`. Pipe it through
ripgrep itself to inspect one entry:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, [Gg][Nn][Uu]makefile, [Mm]akefile, [Mm]akefile.am, ...
```

`--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags you pass in the
same command, so it's the way to confirm a custom type came out the way you

When no built-in type fits, define one with `--type-add`, giving a `name:glob`

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title

You can also build a type out of other types with the `include` directive. It

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc TODO
```

extending it with ordinary globs afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc TODO
```

A related flag, `--type-clear NAME`, wipes the globs previously defined for a
type so you can redefine it from scratch; globs you add after it still apply.

### These settings don't persist

`--type-add` (and `--type-clear`) affect only the current invocation. ripgrep
never saves a custom type to disk. To make one permanent, put it in a shell
alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add a line to your ripgrep configuration file:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the value `all`, standing in for every
type ripgrep knows, including ones you added on the command line. `--type all`
searches in whitelist mode: only files ripgrep recognizes by extension. That has
an edge: a file with no extension, like a bare `my-shell-script`, matches no
type's globs, so `-t all` skips it. Conversely, `--type-not all` searches
exactly those unrecognized files — the ones no type claims — which is a quick way
to sweep up extensionless scripts and oddities your type filters would otherwise
miss.

{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

When you search the same kinds of files all day, typing out globs like
`-g '*.rs'` or `-g '*.{c,h}'` gets old fast. ripgrep's file-type filters give
those glob sets a name, so you can write `-trust` instead. This guide covers the
four flags you'll use: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `--type` / `-t`: search only one kind of file

A *type* is just a name attached to one or more globs. `--type rust` (or the
short forms `-t rust` and `-trust`) tells ripgrep to search only files that
match the `rust` type's globs:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

Because a type can bundle several globs, one name often replaces an awkward
pattern. The `cpp` type, for instance, already covers headers and sources, so
`rg 'int main' -tcpp` beats spelling out `-g '*.{c,h}'`.

You can pass `--type` more than once to search several types at once:

```
$ rg TODO -trust -tpython
```

Two things worth knowing about precedence. First, `--type` is a *whitelist*:
once you name a type, ripgrep searches only matching files. Second, the flag has
lower precedence than both the `--glob` flag and any rules in your ignore files,
so a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit `-g` pattern still wins over a type
selection.

## `--type-not` / `-T`: skip a kind of file

The mirror image excludes a type instead of selecting it. `--type-not` (short
forms `-T` and `-Trust`) searches everything *except* the named type:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of this
type." You can mix them freely in one command; each flag is applied in order.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

ripgrep ships with more than two hundred predefined types, generally
corresponding to well-known formats. To see them all, along with the globs that
make up each one, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line as `name: glob, glob, ...`. Pipe it through
ripgrep itself to inspect one entry:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, [Gg][Nn][Uu]makefile, [Mm]akefile, [Mm]akefile.am, ...
```

`--type-list` reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags you pass in the
same command, so it's the way to confirm a custom type came out the way you
intended.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

When no built-in type fits, define one with `--type-add`, giving a `name:glob`
spec. Suppose you often search "web" files — JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. Add one
glob at a time:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

or, more compactly, use a brace pattern in a single spec:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Only one glob can be added per `--type-add`, but you can pass the flag as many
times as you like, and by default new globs are *added* to any existing globs
for that type rather than replacing them. Type names must consist only of
letters or numbers — no punctuation. Note that adding a type doesn't search
anything by itself; you still select it with `-tweb` (or exclude it with `-T`).

You can also build a type out of other types with the `include` directive. It
imports the rules of one or more existing types, separated by commas:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc TODO
```

That makes `src` match everything `cpp`, `py`, and `md` match. You can keep
extending it with ordinary globs afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc TODO
```

A related flag, `--type-clear NAME`, wipes the globs previously defined for a
type so you can redefine it from scratch; globs you add after it still apply.

### These settings don't persist

`--type-add` (and `--type-clear`) affect only the current invocation. ripgrep
never saves a custom type to disk. To make one permanent, put it in a shell
alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add a line to your ripgrep configuration file:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the value `all`, standing in for every
type ripgrep knows, including ones you added on the command line. `--type all`
searches in whitelist mode: only files ripgrep recognizes by extension. That has

type's globs, so `-t all` skips it. Conversely, `--type-not all` searches
exactly those unrecognized files — the ones no type claims — which is a quick way
to sweep up extensionless scripts and oddities your type filters would otherwise
miss.

bare.text:
# File-type filtering in the `ignore` crate

ripgrep's `--type`/`--type-not` machinery lives entirely in the `ignore`
crate, in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs` and `crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`.
It turns named sets of globs (`rust` → `*.rs`) into a matcher that classifies a
path as whitelisted, ignored, or neither. This note covers how definitions are
represented, how the matcher is compiled, and what to watch when editing this
area. The reader is assumed to be reading the crates.

## How definitions are represented

The shipped defaults are a flat static table:

```rust
pub(crate) const DEFAULT_TYPES: &[(&[&str], &[&str])] = &[
    (&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"]),
    (&["rust"], &["*.rs"]),
    ...
];
```

Each entry pairs a slice of *names* (aliases) with a slice of *globs*. The table
must stay sorted lexicographically by first alias; `default_types_are_sorted`
asserts it, and the file header asks you to wrap to 79 columns.

At runtime a single type is a `FileTypeDef { name: String, globs: Vec<String> }`
(`types.rs:146`). Definitions are collected in `TypesBuilder`, which holds a
`HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` keyed by name plus a `Vec<Selection<()>>` of the
select/negate requests made so far.

`add(name, glob)` (`types.rs:417`) is the primitive: it rejects the reserved
name `all` and any name containing a non-alphanumeric character, then appends the
glob to the entry for `name`, creating the entry if absent. `add_defaults`
(`types.rs:482`) simply loops the table and calls `add` for every (name, glob)
pair. Note the consequence for aliases: `["bat", "batch"]` becomes **two
independent `FileTypeDef`s** that happen to share a glob, not one def with two
names.

`add_def(&str)` (`types.rs:442`) is the end-user-facing parser behind
`--type-add`. It splits on `:` and accepts two forms:

- `name:glob` — a root definition, delegating to `add`.
- `name:include:a,b,c` — copies the globs of already-defined types `a,b,c` into
  `name`. It verifies every referenced type exists *before* mutating anything, so
  a bad include fails without leaving a partial definition (see
  `test_invalid_defs`). The copy is a snapshot: later edits to `a` do not
  propagate.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build()` (`types.rs:322`) compiles a `Types`. It walks the
recorded selections in order; for each, it looks up the named def (returning
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType` if missing) and adds every one of that def's globs
to a `globset::GlobSetBuilder`, each built with `literal_separator(true)` so `*`
never crosses a `/`. Two parallel structures are the key to the design:

- `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>` maps each glob's index in the
  `GlobSet` back to `(selection index, glob index within the def)`.
- `has_selected` records whether any non-negated selection exists.

Only globs from *selected or negated* types enter the `GlobSet`. Unselected
definitions live on solely in `defs` (sorted, for `--type-list`); they never
participate in matching. A `Pool<Vec<usize>>` provides reusable scratch buffers
for per-match results.

## How a match is decided

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` (`types.rs:261`) returns `Match<Glob>`:

1. Directories and an empty set yield `Match::None` — types never apply to
   directories.
2. Matching is against the **file name only**, extracted by
   `pathutil::file_name`, not the full path. A pathological path with no name
   yields `Ignore` when something is selected, else `None`.
3. `set.matches_into` fills the scratch buffer with the indices of all matching
   globs, in ascending order (`globset` sorts them). **The last index wins** —
   `matches.last()` — so precedence follows insertion order, i.e. the latest
   selection, and within it the latest glob.
4. That index resolves through `glob_to_selection` to a `Selection`. A negated
   selection produces `Match::Ignore`; otherwise `Match::Whitelist`. Both carry a
   `Glob` naming the responsible `FileTypeDef`.
5. If nothing matched but at least one type was selected, the path is
   `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())` — the "you asked for Rust, this isn't Rust"
   rule. With no selections, an unmatched path is `Match::None`.

In the walker (`dir.rs:399`) this runs only when `!types.is_empty()`. An
`Ignore` short-circuits and excludes the file; a `Whitelist` is remembered but
does not override an earlier ignore-file ignore. The CLI assembles all of this

# File-type filtering in the `ignore` crate

File-type filtering is what lets you write `rg -trust` to search only Rust
files, or `rg -Tjs` to skip JavaScript. It lives entirely in
`crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with the shipped definitions in
`default_types.rs`. If you're reading the crates, everything below is in those
two files plus the walk in `dir.rs`.

## How a definition is represented

A file type is a `FileTypeDef`: a `name: String` and a `globs: Vec<String>`.
Nothing more. The name is an identifier like `rust` or `c`, and the globs are
plain glob strings that recognize the type by file name. The globs are not
restricted to `*.ext`. A definition can list a literal file name
(`CMakeLists.txt`, `BUILD`, `alire.toml`) or a bracket class (`*.[chH]`), and a
type usually carries several.

The shipped set is `DEFAULT_TYPES`, a `&[(&[&str], &[&str])]` in
`default_types.rs`. Each entry is a tuple of names and globs, for example
`(&["bat", "batch"], &["*.bat"])`. The first slice holds aliases: every name in
it becomes its own `FileTypeDef` sharing the same globs, so `bat` and `batch`
are two definitions that happen to match the same paths. Note that this list
must stay sorted lexicographically by the first alias, and a test
(`default_types_are_sorted`) fails the build if it isn't. The file also asks you
to wrap to 79 columns.

## Building a matcher

You don't construct `Types` directly. You feed a `TypesBuilder`, which holds a
`HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>` of known definitions and a `Vec<Selection<()>>`
of the choices you've made.

- `add_defaults()` loads `DEFAULT_TYPES`, calling `add(name, glob)` once per
  name and glob.
- `add(name, glob)` appends a glob to a definition. The name must be
  alphanumeric and can't be `all`, or you get `Error::InvalidDefinition`.
- `add_def(def)` takes the string form an end user types. `{name}:{glob}` adds a
  root definition. `{name}:include:{a,b,c}` copies the globs of already-defined
  types `a`, `b`, `c` into a new one. Include checks every referenced type
  exists before it changes anything, so a bad reference fails fast and leaves
  the builder untouched.
- `select(name)` and `negate(name)` record a `Selection::Select` or
  `Selection::Negate`. The special name `all` expands to every currently defined
  type.

`build()` turns this into a `Types`. It walks the selections in order, looks
each one up (an unknown name is `Error::UnrecognizedFileType`, raised here
rather than at selection time), and adds every glob to a `GlobSetBuilder` with
`literal_separator(true)`. Alongside the set it records `glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>`,
mapping each glob's index in the compiled `GlobSet` back to the selection it
came from and its position within that definition. It also sets `has_selected`
if any selection is a `Select` rather than a `Negate`. That flag is the whole
game for the "only these types" behavior.

## How matching works

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns a `Match<Glob>`. File types don't apply
to directories, so a directory or an empty set returns `Match::None` at once.
Otherwise it extracts the file name (matching is on the basename, never the full
path) and runs it through `GlobSet::matches_into`, which fills a pooled
`Vec<usize>` of matching glob indices. The pool (`Arc<Pool<Vec<usize>>>`) is
reused scratch space, which keeps `matched` on `&self` and cheap to call across
threads.

The highest-precedent match is the last index in that vector. ripgrep maps it
back through `glob_to_selection` to the selection: a negated selection yields
`Match::Ignore`, a positive one `Match::Whitelist`. Because the last match wins,
selection order decides conflicts, which is how `--type rust --type-not foo`
resolves a path both would claim.

If nothing matched, `has_selected` breaks the tie. With at least one positive
selection, an unmatched path is `Match::Ignore(Glob::unmatched())`, so selecting
`rust` excludes everything that isn't Rust. With only negations, an unmatched
path is `Match::None` and stays a candidate.

In the walk (`dir.rs`), types sit below overrides and gitignore rules. A type
`Ignore` excludes the path, but a type `Whitelist` is only recorded, so a
gitignored file a type whitelists still stays ignored.

## For a contributor changing this area

- Adding a default type means editing `DEFAULT_TYPES`. Keep it sorted by the
  first alias and wrapped to 79 columns, or the sort test or a reviewer will
  catch it.
- Names are alphanumeric and `all` is reserved.
- `include` copies globs at definition time. It's a snapshot, so editing the
  source type afterward doesn't propagate.
- The CLI wiring is in `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types`, which calls
  `add_defaults` then replays `--type-clear`, `--type-add`, `-t/--type` and
  `-T/--type-not` in order. Order matters, so preserve it if you touch that
  loop.

What it covers, and where each claim comes from:

Plus how `dir.rs` consumes it and how `Glob::file_type_def()`/`Types::definitions()` report matches.

# File Type Filtering in ripgrep

If you search text for a living, ripgrep's file-type system turns repetitive glob patterns into single short flags. This guide covers `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`, and shows how to use them effectively.

## What Are File Types?

A file type in ripgrep is a named set of glob patterns that match file names. ripgrep ships with built-in types for dozens of languages and formats: `rust` (matches `*.rs`), `python` (matches `*.py`), `c` (matches `*.c` and `*.h`), and so on. Each type name corresponds to one or more glob patterns. Instead of writing `rg pattern -g '*.rs'` each time you want to search Rust files, you can write `rg pattern --type rust` or the short form `rg pattern -trust`.

## Listing Available Types

`--type-list` shows all types ripgrep recognizes, including any custom types you've defined:

```bash
rg --type-list
```

The output lists each type with its globs. For example:

```
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
rust: *.rs
```

Run this command to discover what types are available before using `--type` or `--type-not`.

## Including Specific File Types: `--type`

`--type TYPE` (short form: `-t TYPE`) tells ripgrep to search *only* files that match a particular type. This puts ripgrep in "whitelist" mode: it ignores everything that doesn't match the types you specify.

```bash
# Search only Rust files
rg 'fn main' --type rust

# Search only Python files (short form)
rg 'def main' -tpy

# Search Rust and Python files (multiple types)
rg 'main' -trust -tpython
```

You can combine short flags: `-trust` is equivalent to `--type rust`. If you provide multiple `--type` flags, ripgrep searches files matching *any* of those types (logical OR).

The short form `-t` takes a TYPE name as its value. You can abbreviate: `-trust` selects the `rust` type; `-tpython` selects the `python` type.

### The Special `all` Type

`--type all` (or `-tall`) selects *every* file type ripgrep knows about. This is useful when combined with other filtering to move from ripgrep's default mixed-mode to explicit whitelist mode:

```bash
# Search only in recognized file types
# (This excludes files with no extension, .gitignore rules, hidden files, etc.)
rg pattern --type all
```

## Excluding Specific File Types: `--type-not`

`--type-not TYPE` (short form: `-T TYPE`) tells ripgrep to skip files matching a type. This puts ripgrep in "blacklist" mode: it searches everything *except* the types you exclude.

```bash
# Search everything except JSON files
rg 'TODO' --type-not json

# Exclude JavaScript (short form)
rg 'TODO' -Tjs

# Exclude multiple types
rg 'console' -Tjs -Tjson -Tyaml
```

The short form `-T` works like `-t`, but negates instead: `-Trust` excludes Rust files.

### The Special `all` Type in Negation

`--type-not all` (or `-Tall`) excludes *every* recognized file type. This is the inverse of `--type all`: it searches only files ripgrep doesn't recognize—files with no extension, custom file formats, or anything outside ripgrep's built-in type definitions.

```bash
# Find matches only in unrecognized files
rg pattern --type-not all
```

## Defining Custom Types: `--type-add`

`--type-add TYPESPEC` adds a custom file type for the current search. A TYPESPEC has the form `name:glob`. You can add multiple glob patterns to the same type by using multiple `--type-add` flags.

```bash
# Add a single glob
rg 'function' --type-add 'my-type:*.mt' -tmy-type

# Add multiple globs to the same type
rg pattern \
  --type-add 'web:*.html' \
  --type-add 'web:*.css' \
  --type-add 'web:*.js' \
  -tweb

# Use glob expansion
rg pattern --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb
```

Custom types are **not persisted** across invocations. If you want a type available in every search, either use a shell alias or add the `--type-add` line to your ripgrep configuration file.

### Composing Types with Include

You can build a custom type from other types using the `include:` directive:

```bash
# Create a 'source' type that includes C++, Python, and Markdown
rg pattern --type-add 'source:include:cpp,py,md' -tsource
```

This imports all glob patterns from the named types. You can still add more globs after including:

```bash
# Include multiple types and add a custom glob
rg pattern \
  --type-add 'source:include:cpp,py' \
  --type-add 'source:*.md' \
  -tsource
```

Type names must contain only alphanumeric Unicode characters (letters and numbers). Punctuation is not allowed, and you cannot name a type `all` (that's reserved).

## Persisting Type Definitions

Because `--type-add` only affects the current invocation, you have two options for persistent types:

**Option 1: Shell alias**

```bash
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

**Option 2: Configuration file**

Set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to point to a config file, then add your type definitions:

```bash
# In ~/.ripgreprc (or wherever you point RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH)
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}

--type-add
config:*.yaml

--type-add
config:*.toml
```

Configuration files apply on every invocation and are the recommended approach.

## Precedence

File type filtering has *lower* precedence than glob patterns (`-g`/`--glob`) and ignore-file rules. This means:

- If you specify `--type rust` but also use `-g '!*.rs'`, the glob pattern wins and no files are searched.
- If you specify `--type python` but your `.gitignore` excludes `.py` files, the `.gitignore` rule wins.
- Ignore-file rules always take precedence over type selections.

## Practical Examples for Text Searchers

**Find all TODO comments in source code only:**

```bash
rg 'TODO' --type-add 'src:include:rust,py,js,go' -tsrc
```

**Search all configuration files:**

```bash
rg 'database_url' --type-add 'config:*.{yaml,yml,toml,ini,conf}' -tconfig
```

**Find a function in C/C++ headers only:**

```bash
rg 'int malloc' -T c -t cpp  # Search C++ but not C
# or
rg 'int malloc' --type-add 'headers:*.{h,hpp}' -theaders
```

**Exclude build artifacts and dependencies:**

```bash
rg 'import' -Tjson -Tyaml -Txml
```

**Search only recognized file types (strict mode):**

```bash
rg pattern --type all  # Won't match .gitignored files or unrecognized formats
```

**Find false positives from a previous search:**

```bash
# First search found matches in config files by accident
rg 'myvar' --type rust  # Search only Rust; config files excluded
```

## Short Forms Reference

| Long Form | Short Form | Meaning |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| `--type rust` | `-trust` | Search only Rust files |
| `--type-not python` | `-Tpython` | Exclude Python files |
| `-t rust -t python` | `-trust -tpython` | Search Rust or Python |
| `-T rust -T python` | `-Trust -Tpython` | Exclude Rust and Python |

Multiple type selections combine: `-trust -tpython` searches both Rust and Python files. Multiple exclusions also combine: `-Trust -Tjson` excludes both Rust and JSON.

## Summary

File types transform glob patterns into single keystrokes. Use `--type-list` to explore what's available, `--type` to search specific formats, `--type-not` to skip them, and `--type-add` to define your own. For regular searchers, these flags save dozens of keystrokes daily and make searches more readable and maintainable.

# File-Type Filtering in ripgrep

When you search text for a living, you spend a lot of time narrowing your focus. You want to find patterns in Python files, or exclude JavaScript when you're searching a monorepo, or search only configuration files. ripgrep's file-type filtering helps you do this—not by writing out glob patterns each time, but by using named types that bundle those globs together.

## How File Types Work

A file type in ripgrep is a named category that corresponds to one or more file-name globs. For example, the `rust` type matches any file ending in `.rs`. The `c` type matches both `*.c` and `*.h` files. ripgrep ships with dozens of built-in types covering common languages and formats.

Rather than write:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
```

You can write:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

Or more concisely:

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The short form `-t` is followed immediately by the type name, with no space. The same applies to `--type-not` with the short form `-T`.

## Include Files with --type

Use `--type` (or `-t`) to search only files matching a given type. This is useful when you're looking for something specific to a language and don't want results from other file types.

For example, to find all function definitions in your C source code:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

This searches only `.c` and `.h` files. You can combine multiple `--type` flags:

```
$ rg 'import' -tpy -tjs
```

This searches Python and JavaScript files, but not Rust or Go.

There's a special type called `all`. When you use `--type all`, ripgrep searches in "whitelist" mode—it will only search files it recognizes via its type definitions. This means files without recognized extensions won't be searched.

```
$ rg pattern --type all
```

will search only known file types, skipping untyped files like shell scripts without a `.sh` extension.

Note that `--type` has lower precedence than glob patterns (`-g`) and ignore-file rules (`.gitignore`, `.ignore`). This means if you exclude a file with a glob or ignore rule, a type filter won't override that exclusion.

## Exclude Files with --type-not

Use `--type-not` (or `-T`) to exclude files of a specific type from your search. This is the inverse of `--type`: you search everything except the named type.

For example, to search your codebase but exclude all test files:

```
$ rg pattern --type-not test
```

More concisely:

```
$ rg pattern -Ttest
```

You can stack multiple type exclusions:

```
$ rg pattern -Ttest -Tdocs
```

Like `--type`, there's a special value `all`. Using `--type-not all` causes ripgrep to search in "blacklist" mode—it will only search files that are *not* recognized by its type definitions.

```
$ rg pattern --type-not all
```

This searches only untyped files (files without recognized extensions), which is useful if you want to find patterns in loose scripts or generated files that don't have a standard extension.

## List Available Types with --type-list

To see what file types ripgrep knows about and what globs they match, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

This prints every type and its globs, one type per line, in the format:

```
rust: *.rs
c: *.c, *.h
python: *.py, *.pyw
```

The output respects any custom types you've defined with `--type-add` or cleared with `--type-clear`, so it always reflects the types available for the current command.

If you want to find a specific type, pipe to ripgrep itself:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
```

## Add Custom Types with --type-add

ripgrep comes with built-in types for most languages and formats, but you can define your own. Use `--type-add` to add a glob pattern to a type (either an existing type or a new one).

For example, to create a type called `web` that matches HTML, CSS, and JavaScript:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

This is more concisely written using brace expansion:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Each `--type-add` takes a single specification in the form `TYPE:GLOB`. By default, when you add a type, the globs are *added* to any existing globs for that type. If the type doesn't exist, it's created. If it does exist (like `python`), your new globs are appended.

### Including Other Types

You can also compose types by including other types. Use the special `include:` directive to inherit all globs from one or more existing types:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' pattern
```

This creates a type called `src` that matches C++, Python, and Markdown files. You can then add more globs to it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc pattern
```

The `src` type now matches the globs from `cpp`, `py`, and `md`, plus `*.foo` files.

### Important: Types Are Per-Command

Type definitions created with `--type-add` apply *only* to that ripgrep invocation. They're not saved anywhere. The next time you run ripgrep, your custom types are gone unless you specify them again.

If you use the same custom types repeatedly, add them to your ripgrep configuration file. Set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to point to a config file, then add lines like:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
--type-add=src:include:cpp,py,md
```

Each line is a separate flag argument, just as if you'd typed it on the command line.

Alternatively, create a shell alias:

```bash
alias rg="rg --type-add='web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

## Type Names

Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers. Punctuation and underscores are not allowed. Keep them short and memorable: `rust`, `py`, `js`, `web`, `doc`.

## How Globs Work

File-type globs behave the same way as `.gitignore` globs. They're matched against the file name (including the path). If you write `*.rs`, it matches any file ending in `.rs`. If you write `src/*.py`, it matches Python files in a `src` directory. Globs can use:

- `*` to match any sequence of characters (except `/`)
- `?` to match a single character
- `[abc]` to match any character in the set
- `{a,b,c}` to match any of the alternatives

## Real-World Examples

**Search for TODO comments only in source code, not tests:**

```
$ rg 'TODO' -tsrc
```

(assuming you've defined a `src` type with your source extensions)

**Search a monorepo for configuration changes, excluding all code:**

```
$ rg 'timeout' --type-add 'conf:*.yaml,*.yml,*.toml,*.json' -tconf
```

**Find all function names in Go and Rust files:**

```
$ rg '(?P<name>\w+)\s*\(' -tgo -trust
```

**Search everything except tests and documentation:**

```
$ rg pattern -Ttest -Tdocs
```

**Search only untyped files (scripts without extensions):**

```
$ rg pattern --type-not all
```

## When to Use Type Filtering

Use `--type` when you know exactly what file type you want. It's fast because ripgrep can skip everything else.

Use `--type-not` when you want to exclude just a few types but keep most others. It's often faster than adding many `--type` flags.

Use custom types with `--type-add` when your codebase has non-standard extensions or when you want to group unrelated files together (like the `web` example).

Always check `--type-list` to see what's already defined before creating custom types. ripgrep likely already has a type for what you're searching.

Remember: type filtering works alongside all of ripgrep's other filtering. Files excluded by `.gitignore`, hidden files, and binary files are all filtered independently. Type filtering adds one more layer of control.

# ripgrep File-Type Filtering

When you search files for a living, you often want to limit your search to a particular category of files. ripgrep provides a powerful system for filtering by file type: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## Understanding File Types

A file type in ripgrep is a named collection of glob patterns that match files. For example, the built-in `rust` type matches `*.rs` files, and the `c` type matches C source and header files (`*.c`, `*.h`, and some variants). These types correspond to well-known public formats.

ripgrep ships with dozens of pre-defined types covering everything from `asm` to `zephir`. You don't need to remember the glob patterns—you just use the name.

## `--type`: Include Files of a Specific Type

The `--type` flag (short form: `-t`) tells ripgrep to search only files matching a given type. Multiple `--type` flags can be combined to search multiple types at once.

### Basic Usage

To search only Rust files:

```bash
rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

Or use the short form:

```bash
rg 'fn run' -trus
```

To search both Rust and Python files:

```bash
rg 'def ' --type rust --type python
```

### The `all` Special Value

Ripgrep recognizes a special type name: `all`. When you use `--type all`, ripgrep searches files matching *any* known type. This puts ripgrep into "whitelist" mode, where it only recognizes files according to its type definitions.

```bash
rg pattern --type all
```

This is useful when you want ripgrep to ignore unrecognized files entirely.

## `--type-not`: Exclude Files of a Specific Type

The `--type-not` flag (short form: `-T`) does the opposite: it excludes files of a given type from the search.

### Basic Usage

To search everything except Rust files:

```bash
rg 'clap' --type-not rust
```

Or use the short form:

```bash
rg 'clap' -Trust
```

Multiple exclusions combine:

```bash
rg 'import' --type-not rust --type-not python
```

### The `all` Special Value with Type-Not

Using `--type-not all` puts ripgrep into "blacklist" mode. It searches only files that are *not recognized* by any type definition—effectively searching only files with unknown extensions or names.

```bash
rg pattern --type-not all
```

## `--type-list`: Discover Available Types

To see all available file types and their corresponding glob patterns, use `--type-list`:

```bash
rg --type-list
```

This prints output like:

```
rust: *.rs
python: *.py, *.pyw, *.pyi
c: *.[chH], *.[chH].in, *.cats
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

Each type appears on its own line, followed by a colon and a comma-delimited list of glob patterns.

## `--type-add`: Define Custom File Types

The `--type-add` flag lets you define new file types (or extend existing ones) for the current command.

### Basic Usage

Define a type for a single glob pattern:

```bash
rg --type-add 'foo:*.foo' -tfoo pattern
```

Or define a type that matches multiple patterns:

```bash
rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb 'title'
```

You can add multiple globs to the same type by using `--type-add` multiple times:

```bash
rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb 'title'
```

### Composition with Include Directives

A more advanced feature: you can compose types by including the globs from other types. Use the special `include:` directive:

```bash
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc pattern
```

This creates a type called `src` that includes all globs from the `cpp`, `py`, and `md` types. You can still add more globs afterward:

```bash
rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc pattern
```

Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers. Punctuation is not allowed.

## Important Limitations

Type definitions added with `--type-add` apply **only to the current command**. They are not saved or persisted anywhere. If you want a custom type available in every ripgrep invocation, use one of two approaches:

1. **Shell alias**: Create an alias in your shell configuration:
   ```bash
   alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
   ```

2. **Configuration file**: Add `--type-add` arguments to a ripgrep configuration file. Set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to point to this file. For example, in `~/.ripgreprc`:
   ```
   --type-add
   web:*.{html,css,js}
   ```
   Then export `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH=$HOME/.ripgreprc`.

## Precedence and Interaction with Other Filters

The `--type` flag has lower precedence than both glob patterns (specified with `--glob`) and rules found in `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` files. This means:

- If you use both `--type` and `--glob`, the most restrictive rule wins.
- If a file matches a type but is excluded by `.gitignore`, it will not be searched.

## Combining Types with Globs

You can combine type filtering with traditional glob patterns for fine-grained control:

```bash
rg pattern --type rust -g '!vendor/*'
```

This searches only Rust files but explicitly excludes anything in the `vendor` directory.

## Summary

- **`--type TYPE`** (`-tTYPE`): Search only files of the given type.
- **`--type-not TYPE`** (`-TTYPE`): Exclude files of the given type.
- **`--type-add TYPESPEC`**: Define or extend a type for this command only.
- **`--type-list`**: Display all available types and their glob patterns.

These flags form ripgrep's answer to the question "which files should I search?"—a question that recurs constantly when you search text for a living.
